content: The purpose of this document is to provide detailed information about rabies to veterinarians, public health officials, and others involved in rabies prevention and control. These recommendations form the foundation for animal rabies control programs across the United States and aim to standardize procedures among jurisdictions, thereby contributing to an effective national rabies control program. The document is reviewed annually and updated as necessary. Part I: Recommendations for Parenteral Vaccination Procedures A. Vaccine Administration All animal rabies vaccines should only be administered by, or under the direct supervision of, a licensed veterinarian. B. Vaccine Selection Part II of the document lists all rabies vaccines licensed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and available in the United States at the time of publication. Any new vaccine approvals or changes to label specifications after publication should also be considered part of this list. Vaccines used in state and local rabies control programs should provide immunity for at least three years, as this is the most effective way to increase the proportion of immunized dogs and cats in a population. C. Route of Inoculation All vaccines must be administered according to the specifications provided on the product label or package insert. D. Wildlife and Hybrid Animal Vaccination The efficacy of parenteral rabies vaccination in wildlife and hybrid animals (offspring of wild animals crossbred with domestic dogs or cats) has not been established, and no vaccines are licensed for these animals. Zoos or research institutions may implement vaccination programs to protect valuable animals, but these programs should not replace public health measures designed to protect humans. E. Accidental Human Exposure to Vaccine Human exposure to parenteral animal rabies vaccines listed in Part II does not pose a risk of rabies infection. However, any human exposure to vaccinia-vectored oral rabies vaccines should be reported to state health officials. F. Identification of Vaccinated Animals Agencies and veterinarians may use a standardized tag system to verify the rabies vaccination status of animals. Registration or licensure of dogs, cats, and ferrets can also aid in rabies control, with fees often used to support rabies or animal control programs. Postexposure Management Dogs, Cats, and Ferrets Unvaccinated dogs, cats, and ferrets exposed to a rabid animal should be euthanized immediately. If the owner refuses, the animal should be placed in strict isolation for six months and vaccinated one month before release. Animals with expired vaccinations should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Currently vaccinated animals should be revaccinated immediately, kept under the owner’s control, and observed for 45 days. Livestock Livestock exposed to a rabid animal and currently vaccinated with a USDA-approved vaccine should be revaccinated immediately and observed for 45 days. Unvaccinated livestock should be slaughtered immediately. If the owner refuses, the animal should be closely observed for six months. If an unvaccinated animal is slaughtered within seven days of being bitten, its tissues may be consumed safely, provided the exposed area is discarded. Federal meat inspectors must reject animals exposed to rabies within eight months. Milk or tissues from a rabid animal should not be consumed. Pasteurization inactivates the rabies virus, so drinking pasteurized milk or eating cooked meat does not constitute rabies exposure. Other Animals Mammals bitten by a rabid animal should be euthanized immediately. Animals in USDA-licensed research facilities or accredited zoological parks should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Management of Animals That Bite Humans Dogs, Cats, and Ferrets A healthy dog, cat, or ferret that bites a person should be confined and observed daily for 10 days. Rabies vaccination is not recommended during this period. Any signs of illness should be reported immediately to the local health department. If rabies is suspected, the animal should be euthanized, and its head submitted for laboratory examination. Stray or unwanted dogs, cats, or ferrets that bite a person may be euthanized immediately, and their heads submitted for rabies testing. Other Biting Animals Any other biting animals that may have exposed a person to rabies should be reported immediately to the local health department. Prior vaccination of the animal does not eliminate the need for euthanasia and testing if the period of virus shedding is unknown for that species. Management depends on the species, circumstances of the bite, local rabies epidemiology, and the animal’s health and exposure history. Control Methods Among Wildlife The public should be warned not to handle wildlife. Wild mammals and hybrids that bite or expose humans, pets, or livestock should be considered for euthanasia and rabies testing. Individuals bitten by wild mammals should report the incident to a physician for evaluation of the need for postexposure prophylaxis. Wildlife rehabilitators may play a role in rabies control programs, but they should meet minimum standards, including rabies vaccination, appropriate training, and continuing education. Translocation of infected wildlife has contributed to the spread of rabies; therefore, moving known terrestrial rabies reservoir species should be prohibited. Terrestrial Mammals Licensed oral vaccines for mass vaccination of free-ranging wildlife may be used in specific situations with state agency approval. Continuous government-funded programs for trapping or poisoning wildlife are not cost-effective for reducing rabies reservoirs on a statewide basis. Bats Rabid bats have been reported in every state except Hawaii and have caused rabies in at least 33 humans in the United States. Bats should be excluded from homes and adjacent structures to prevent direct contact with humans. Structures should be sealed to prevent bat entry. Programs to reduce bat populations are neither feasible nor desirable for rabies control.
